## Part 2: Topic and Data

### Context of the problem to be analyzed:

The problem to be analyzed is the relationship between the financial burden of higher education (specifically the ratio of financial aid to tuition costs) and student outcomes (specifically graduation rates). The analysis will test the assumption that a decrease in financial aid relative to tuition costs negatively impacts graduation rates, and that the COVID-19 pandemic likely exacerbated these negative effects.

This analysis is important for understanding equity and accessibility in U.S. higher education. By examining detailed breakdowns by race, gender, and institutional categories (like HBCUs or religious affiliations), the project can highlight how financial pressures disparately affect different demographic groups and institutional types.

The scope of this project covers U.S. colleges and universities using data from the past 10 years. The analysis will be national in scope, with the ability to filter data for any school in the country, allowing for detailed breakdowns by race and gender for each race, as well as by institutional characteristics.

The primary goal is to develop an application that allows users to visualize and explore these financial-to-outcome ratios. The analysis will specifically focus on visualizing 10-year trends and correlating the changes in aid-to-tuition ratios with corresponding changes in graduation rates.

### Literature Review:

1: Loeb, Susanna, and Marianne E. Page. "Examining the Link Between Teacher Wages and Student Outcomes: The Importance of Alternative Labor Market Opportunities and Non-Pecuniary Variation." *The Review of Economics and Statistics*, vol. 82, no. 3, Aug. 2000, pp. 393-408. *Stanford CEPA*, <https://cepa.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/loebpage.pdf>.

The relationship between university resources and student success is complex, as studies often fail to find a consistent link between per-pupil spending and better outcomes. A study by Susanna Loeb and Marianne E. Page argues this is because previous research overlooked key variables, especially alternative labor market opportunities. They found that a high salary alone doesn't attract the best educators if other, more lucrative professions are available. By creating a “relative wage” measure that compares teacher salaries to those of other local professionals, Loeb and Page isolated the true effect of compensation. After controlling for external factors, they found a 10% increase in relative teacher wages reduces high school dropout rates by 3% to 4%. This demonstrates that competitive salaries *do* positively impact student retention. This study provides a strong framework for our project, suggesting we should investigate whether universities that invest more in faculty, relative to their local labor market, see higher graduation rates, especially when considering student preparedness.

2: Heil, S., Reisel, L., & Attewell, P. (2014). College Selectivity and Degree Completion. American Educational Research Journal, 51(5), 913–935. <https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831214544298>

College Selectivity and Degree Completion, by Scott Heil, Liza Reisel, and Paul Attewell looked at if college selectivity affected a college student’s likelihood of graduation. This paper measured if a student were to graduate college within 6 years of starting, and used many predictors including SAT selectivity and tuition. They adjusted for likelihood of attending a college or a certain level and then compared how different predictors were associated with chances of graduation. They found graduation rates were largely affected by the makeup of the student body and by high tuition. They concluded that selectivity of a college does affect graduation rates to a very small extent, but that there is weak evidence that the chance of graduation for students who would struggle to graduate would improve if they attended a more selective college. Our project includes data on many US colleges and a big variable we are looking at is graduation numbers. It is helpful to know that selectivity of the school likely doesn’t play a key role in a student graduating, but it would be interesting to look at tuition in correlation to those graduation rates.

3: Hemelt, Steven W., and Dave E. Marcotte. “The Impact of Tuition Increases on Enrollment at Public Colleges and Universities.” *Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis*, vol. 33, no. 4, Dec. 2011, pp. 435–457. American Educational Research Association. <https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373711415261>

The study by Steven W. Hemelt and Dave E. Marcotte (2011) provides foundational insight into how tuition costs affect enrollment at public universities. Using IPEDS data, they found that a \$100 tuition increase leads to a \~0.25% enrollment decline, an effect most pronounced at Research I universities. The study also highlights that financial aid, especially Pell Grants, can mitigate these negative effects; Pell funding had a stronger positive impact on enrollment than tuition had a negative one. However, Hemelt and Marcotte note that lower-income students and those at less selective institutions are more sensitive to these financial changes. This research directly informs our project, as it provides an empirical basis for our hypothesis: if declining aid relative to tuition lowers enrollment, it will also negatively impact graduation rates. Their findings reinforce the importance of tracking the aid-to-tuition ratio over time, especially when analyzing institutional differences and demographic inequities.

### Proposed Data Source:

Our data comes from: <https://ies.ed.gov/> - Institute of Education Sciences

We pulled data from 2013-2023. The website allows for selection from various data sets with various filters. The website only allows you to select one year at a time but we combined data sets to have 5.

**Characteristics data:** 2208 rows, 11 columns; contains the school names and characteristics.

**Enrollment data:** 371882 rows, 6 columns; contains enrollment data of each college with different demographic data.

**Financial aid data**: 88321 rows, 6 columns; contains each college and relevant aid types and amounts.

**Grad data:** 677501 rows, 8 columns; contains number of graduated students in each college with a few demographics.

**Tuition data:** 495059 rows, 5 columns; contains both in and out of state tuition for each university.

## Part 3: Use Case

### Use Case & Actor Description

Our primary actors are prospective students and parents and researchers, either for institutions themselves or for policy making. The prospective students and parents are motivated by a practical need to find the "best value" college; their goal is to use our app's demographic filters (race, gender) to see the 10-year aid-to-tuition ratios and graduation rates for students like them. The researchers are motivated by a research need; their goal is to use our app's institutional filters (e.g., HBCU, Public/Private) to identify systemic trends and use the statistical analysis features to find evidence for how financial aid correlate with student outcomes. The app's workflow directly serves both actors' goals. The prospective students and parents will filter for a specific school and demographic, then visually compare the multi-year trend lines for the aid-to-tuition ratio and graduation rates to inform their enrollment decision. The researchers will take this one step further and after filtering for a group of institutions, they will click the "Run Statistical Analysis" button to quantify the visual trend. This provides them with a correlation coefficient and regression output, allowing them to statistically test the hypothesis that changes in financial aid are directly associated with changes in graduation rates for that institutional category

### Actor Questions of Interest

Our app could help users answer four types of questions:

1.  **Data Look up:** What are the current tuition, average financial aid, and graduation rates at a specific school?

2.  **Trend Analysis:** How have these metrics (especially the aid-to-tuition ratio and graduation rates) changed over the last 10 years?

3.  **Equity Analysis:** How do these trends differ for specific groups based on race, gender, or institutional type (like HBCU or religious affiliation)?

4.  **Hypothesis Testing:** Is there a statistically significant correlation between the financial aid-to-tuition ratio and graduation rates for a given school or demographic?

### Anticipated Workflow for the Actor

The user first filters the app by a specific school or by institutional categories (e.g., State, HBCU, Public/Private). The app loads and displays a 10-year line chart comparing the Aid-to-Tuition Ratio and the 6-Year Graduation Rate. The user can then apply demographic filters (`Race`, `Gender`), which instantly updates the chart for that subgroup. After forming a visual hypothesis (e.g., "it looks like aid and grad rates are related"), the user clicks "Run Statistical Analysis." The app then runs a correlation and linear regression on the 10 data points and displays a plain-English summary of the Correlation Coefficient (r-value), the Regression Model (e.g., "a #% aid increase was associated with a #.## point grad rate increase"), and the R-squared. This allows the user to move from a visual guess to a quantitative conclusion, confirming whether the relationship between aid and outcomes is statistically significant for their selected group.

## Part 4: Ethical Review

The *College Cost & Completion* project requires our group to responsibly handle public, de-identified IES data (2013-2023) by maintaining fairness, accuracy, and transparency throughout the data life cycle. Because the data show patterns tied to race, gender, and institution type, we will interpret results cautiously, avoid overstating causation, and label all visualizations to prevent bias. Our work adheres to professional guidelines, primarily the ACM Code of Ethics (honesty, responsibility, fairness) and the American Statistical Association (ASA) guidelines, which promote transparency, clear citation of methods, and acknowledging uncertainty in our findings. Team collaboration and integrity are enforced using GitHub for version control, ensuring all changes are logged and peer-reviewed. By following these ACM and ASA principles, our team ensures the project remains fair and transparent from collection to presentation.

## Part 5: App Concept

### Layout of the App

Our application will be a single-page, interactive dashboard with a two-column layout: a Left Sidebar (Control Panel) and a Main Area (Dashboard Display). This single-page design ensures a seamless workflow, keeping the visual trends and statistical analysis clearly connected. The Control Panel will contain all user inputs: a School Search Bar, Institutional Filters (Control, State, HBCU, Religious, Urbanization), and Year Selection check boxes. The main Dashboard Display will feature a Demographic Filter Bar (`Race`/`Gender`) at the top, followed by the Main Trend Visualization (an interactive line chart with hover-over tool tips). Positioned directly below the chart is the Statistical Analysis Card, where a "Run Statistical Analysis" button will generate a plain-English summary of the correlation, regression, and R-Squared. Finally, an interactive data table viewer will be placed at the bottom for users to see the raw data for themselves.

### User Data Selection and Manipulation

Users will begin by searching for a specific institution or applying filters such as year, state, control (public/private), or institutional type (e.g., HBCU, religious affiliation). Once selected, the app dynamically pulls data from the five combined data sets, Characteristics, Enrollment, Financial Aid, Graduation, and Tuition, sourced from the Institute of Education Sciences (2013–2023). The system automatically merges these data sets by institutional ID and cleans them by removing duplicates, aligning formats, and addressing missing values. Key variables such as the Aid-to-Tuition Ratio and Graduation Rate are then calculated for each institution and demographic group. Users can refine their view by filtering for specific races or genders, selecting custom year ranges, or choosing to log-transform numerical columns (like tuition or aid) for smoother trend visualization. The resulting filtered data set instantly updates the dashboard’s charts and statistical outputs, ensuring accurate, real-time exploration of relationships between financial aid, tuition, and graduation outcomes.

### User Exploratory Numerical/Graphical Analysis

Our EDA will focus on identifying structural patterns, temporal trends, and demographic disparities in the data, with a specific focus on the COVID-19 pandemic's impact. We will use time-series plots to visualize how key financial indicators (tuition, financial aid) and student outcomes (enrollment, graduation rates) evolved over the decade, marking the pandemic years for disruption analysis. This data will be disaggregated by race, gender, and institutional characteristics (e.g., public/private, HBCU, urban/rural) to examine shifts in access and completion. We will use grouped bar charts, faceted plots, and boxplots to compare these trends across demographic and institutional categories. Finally, scatterplots and correlation matrices will be used to explore the core relationships between financial variables and student outcomes like graduation rates.

### Statistical Models and Tests

To quantitatively test our project's core hypothesis, the app will run two statistical models on the user's filtered 10-year data when they click "Run Statistical Analysis." First, a Pearson Correlation (r-value) will be calculated to provide a single metric (e.g., "r = 0.72, Strong Positive") measuring the strength and direction of the relationship between the aid-to-tuition ratio and graduation rates. Second, a Simple Linear Regression will be run to model this relationship, providing a plain-English interpretation (e.g., "A 1% aid ratio increase was associated with a 0.35 point grad rate increase") and an R-squared value to show how much of the change in outcomes is explained by the change in aid.

### Approach to Team Workflow, collaboration and branching

Our group will use a coordinated approach centered on GitHub for version control and a dedicated message channel for daily communication. We will follow a simplified branching model where the `main` branch is protected and stores only stable, milestone-ready versions. Each team member will conduct all development on their own persistent, personal branch, named after them. When a task or feature is complete, the group member will submit a Pull Request on GitHub to merge their personal branch into the `main` branch. This Pull Request will require review and approval from at least one other group member to ensure code quality, share knowledge, and prevent conflicts. This workflow allows us to work in parallel on our individual branches while ensuring the `main` branch always remains in a functional state. To further avoid merge conflicts, we have implemented a system in a shared doc that allows us to see which part of the project someone is currently working on. This way, two group members will not be overwriting each others code with their work at the same time.
